title: Appointed times
hookLine: the second order: Shabbat, festivals and fasts

lines: COME WITH YOUR STAFF AND YOUR MONEY.
cards: Two great sages disagree about when the new month began. It sounds small. It isn't.

If the month began on a different day, then Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, falls on a different day too. Rabban Gamaliel, head of the court, has fixed the date. Rabbi Joshua is convinced he got it wrong.
So Rabban Gamaliel sends an order: come to me with your walking staff and your money, on the day that by your count is Yom Kippur. On a fast day, you don't travel or carry money.
He is asking Rabbi Joshua to break his own holy day in public. What will Rabbi Joshua do?

teach.h: MOED: THE ORDER OF HOLY TIME.
teach.b: Moed. Appointed time. The second of the six orders is the order of holy time, with tractates named for the days themselves: Shabbat.
Pesachim, for Passover. Yoma, the Day, meaning Yom Kippur. Sukkah.
Rosh Hashanah. Taanit, on fasts. Megillah, on Purim.
Over the coming days you'll open several of them. The name comes from the Torah's own words for the festivals.

teach.h: THE APPOINTED SEASONS, WHICH YE PROCLAIM.
teach.b: In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "These are the appointed seasons of the LORD." And the verse goes on: holy gatherings, which ye shall proclaim. Back to Rabbi Joshua, in tractate Rosh Hashanah.

He is deeply troubled. Rabbi Akiva comes to him with that same verse: the festivals are the ones you proclaim. Whether the court sets the date at the right time or not, these are the appointed seasons.
Another sage adds: if we question every court's ruling, there will be no end to it.

teach.h: RABBI JOSHUA TAKES UP HIS STAFF.
teach.b: So Rabbi Joshua takes his staff and his money and walks to Rabban Gamaliel on the day he himself believed was Yom Kippur.

Rabban Gamaliel stands up, kisses him on the head, and says, in paraphrase: come in peace, my teacher and my student. My teacher in wisdom, my student because you accepted my word. That's what this order is about.
Holy time has rules, and the rules are kept together: a calendar a whole people keeps as one.

how: Jews keep a shared calendar of Shabbat, festivals and fasts, and the laws for each are studied in the tractates of the order Moed; today the Hebrew calendar is fixed by calculation rather than by witnesses to the new moon.

o: a meeting place where the sages held court
appointed time: the order on Shabbat and festivals
a festival when Jews remember the Temple's fall

p: these are the seasons ye proclaim

s: the order of Moed covers only Shabbat
it covers Shabbat, festivals and fasts: Pesachim, Yoma, Sukkah, Rosh Hashanah, Taanit, Megillah and more.
Rabbi Joshua came to Rabban Gamaliel on the day he believed was Yom Kippur
with his staff and his money, and Rabban Gamaliel kissed him on the head.
in the story, Rabbi Joshua turns out to be wrong about the moon
the Mishnah never says who was right. it says the festivals are the ones the court proclaims.

games.q: you're Rabbi Joshua. the head of the court has ordered you to walk to him with your staff and money on the day you believe is Yom Kippur. what do you do?
o: refuse, and keep the fast on your own date.
take your staff and money, and go.
games.why: after Rabbi Akiva reads him the verse, he goes. Rabban Gamaliel stands, kisses his head and calls him my teacher and my student.

practice: Picture the month ahead and look for the times already appointed: a Shabbat, a holiday, a birthday, the anniversary of a loss, a standing dinner with someone you love.

Notice which ones you protect and which get pushed around, and choose one to keep with the steadiness a community keeps its calendar. If you keep Shabbat or the festivals, you might look at how this month's fall.
